item.title: Tunguska event
item.description: The Tunguska event was a large explosion that occurred on the morning of 30 June [O.S. 17 June] 1908, at around 7:14 KRAT (0:14 UT) in Central Siberia, then part of the Russian Empire. This cataclysm occurred in a remote and sparsely populated region of the taiga, near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River after which it is named. The shock wave knocked several witnesses to the ground, killed at least three people as well as numerous animals, and shattered windows within a 200 km (120 mi) radius. The blast was recorded by various Russian and German seismological stations with a magnitude close to 5 on the Richter scale, while atmospheric waves generated by the shock wave were detected worldwide. From 30 June to 3 July, intense bright nights were observed across western Eurasia over an area of more than 10,000,000 km2 (3,900,000 sq mi). Although the Russian press and various correspondents reported the blast in the following days, it was not until 1921 that a first scientific expedition was organized under the direction of Leonid Kulik, who discovered the site of the epicenter only in 1927. Kulik and his successors research revealed that the explosion devastated nearly 2,150 km2 (830 sq mi) of forest in a radial pattern which implied an aerial origin. The scientific consensus thus attributes this event to a meteor air burst, the atmospheric explosion of a celestial body, although no fragment has been formally identified. By cross-referencing eyewitness accounts and physical modeling, researchers favor the hypothesis of a 50–60 m (160–200 ft) diameter meteoroid moving at high speed from south-east. The object would have exploded between 5–10 km (3.1–6.2 mi) in altitude, releasing an energy often estimated between 10 and 15 megatons of TNT, which is enough to destroy an entire major city. This interpretation is reinforced by data collected since the passage of the Chelyabinsk meteor in 2013, whose dynamics were similar. The Tunguska event thus constitutes both the most violent impact event on Earth and one of the most powerful explosions ever documented. However, the exact nature of the object—that is, whether it was an asteroid or a comet—is still debated. Alternative, terrestrial hypotheses, such as the release of explosive underground gas, have also been suggested, though they remain marginal among the scientific community. Lake Cheko, located approximately 8 km (5.0 mi) northeast of the epicenter and unrecorded before 1908, may be an impact crater formed by a secondary fragment of the celestial body that detached before its explosion. While its atypical shape and its orientation along the trajectory axis support this hypothesis, several sedimentary studies support a contrary conclusion. A 2019 study suggested that the explosion may have decimated the breeding population of the Sushkin's goose, contributing to its extinction in the following years. The incident remains the primary historical benchmark for assessing risks associated with near-Earth objects as well as for developing planetary defense strategies, and the explosion site is now protected in a nature reserve. The event is frequently depicted in works of fiction, particularly science fiction, through a wide variety of interpretations.
